Clinical Reference

Hypercalcemia

On this page
Hypercalcemia = a corrected (or ionized) serum calcium above the lab's upper limit — in the outpatient world it's almost always primary hyperparathyroidism; in the hospital it's almost always malignancy. Together those two causes are ~90% of cases.
Corrected Ca = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin) Moderate 12–13.9 mg/dL Severe / crisis ≥14 mg/dL First move: isotonic saline PTH is the pivot lab
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Calcium homeostasis — the three-organ thermostat

~99% of body calcium is locked in bone as hydroxyapatite; the ~1% in serum is what the body regulates minute-to-minute, and about half of that is the biologically active ionized fraction (the rest is bound to albumin or complexed). Three hormones and three organs hold serum calcium in a tight band:

  • PTH (parathyroid) — the master up-regulator. It pulls calcium out of bone (activates osteoclasts via RANKL), reclaims calcium in the distal renal tubule, dumps phosphate in the urine, and switches on renal 1α-hydroxylase to make active vitamin D.
  • Calcitriol (1,25-OH vitamin D) — the up-regulator at the gut: it drives intestinal absorption of both calcium and phosphate.
  • Calcitonin (thyroid C-cells) — a weak brake on osteoclasts; physiologically minor, but a usable drug.

The sensor that ties it together is the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on the parathyroid cell and the renal tubule. When ionized calcium rises, CaSR fires and PTH secretion is shut off. Hypercalcemia is what happens when this loop is broken — either the parathyroid stops listening to the CaSR (adenoma), or calcium enters the blood from a source that ignores PTH entirely (tumor, granuloma, vitamin D, bone turnover).

Two features explain why the same number can mean very different things. First, rate matters as much as level: a calcium that climbs to 12.5 over days (a fast-growing tumor) overwhelms compensation and causes delirium, while a chronic 11.5 from a slow adenoma may be silent. Second, hypercalcemia is self-amplifying through the kidney. A high calcium binds the renal CaSR in the thick ascending limb, which blocks the Na-K-2Cl transporter and downregulates aquaporin-2 — producing an ADH-resistant nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The patient pours out dilute urine, gets dehydrated, and can't drink enough (nausea, confusion). Dehydration drops the GFR, the kidney's one route to dump calcium closes, and the calcium climbs further. Breaking that cycle with saline is why fluids — not a fancy drug — is step one.

Think of serum calcium like the water level in a sink. PTH and vitamin D are the taps (bone, gut, kidney reabsorption); the kidney's calcium excretion is the drain. Hypercalcemia is the sink overflowing — a tap stuck open (an autonomous adenoma or a tumor pouring calcium in) and a clogged drain (dehydration cripples the kidney's ability to excrete it). That's why the very first thing you do is unclog the drain with saline before you worry about turning off the taps.

Calcium enters serum from bone, gut and kidney; four mechanisms drive it too high; dehydration closes a vicious cycle.
Integrated calcium regulation — PTH, calcitriol (1,25-OH vitamin D) and calcitonin acting on bone, gut and kidney.
Mikael Häggström, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain — source

Why each drug class works — mapped to the cascade

Every hypercalcemia drug attacks one specific step above:
  • Isotonic saline restores GFR and, because the renal tubule co-handles sodium and calcium, a high filtered sodium load drags calcium out with it (saline calciuresis) — it re-opens the drain.
  • Calcitonin directly brakes the osteoclast and increases renal calcium excretion — fast but short-lived.
  • Bisphosphonates are swallowed by osteoclasts and poison their farnesyl-pyrophosphate synthase → osteoclast apoptosis → the bone tap is shut for weeks.
  • Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL, so osteoclasts are never recruited in the first place — and it isn't cleared by the kidney.
  • Glucocorticoids shut off macrophage/lymphoma 1α-hydroxylase, dropping calcitriol — they only work on the vitamin-D-driven causes.
  • Cinacalcet is a CaSR agonist — it makes the parathyroid "hear" the high calcium again and turn PTH down.

Watch on Osmosis: Hypercalcemia · Hyperparathyroidism · Calcium homeostasis.

The single most useful split is PTH-mediated vs PTH-independent, because that's exactly what the first lab (intact PTH) tells you.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy is a bad prognostic sign — it signals high tumor burden and historically carries a median survival of only weeks-to-a-few-months. Treating the calcium is important, but it is a marker to revisit goals of care.

How it presents

🔍

"Stones, bones, groans, thrones & psychiatric moans"

Most outpatient hypercalcemia is mild and asymptomatic — a calcium of 10.6–11.5 flagged on a routine metabolic panel. Symptoms track both the level and the rate of rise: a chronic 11.5 can feel fine while an acute 12.5 causes delirium. Frequencies below are approximate and pooled across severities.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Asymptomatic (incidental)~50–80% of mild PHPTLevel too low / too chronic to overwhelm the kidney's calcium buffer
Fatigue, weakness, malaise~40–60%Calcium blunts neuromuscular excitability and cellular energy handling
Polyuria & polydipsia~40–50% (moderate+)Nephrogenic DI — Ca activates the tubular CaSR, downregulating aquaporin-2 & the TAL Na-K-2Cl transporter → ADH-resistant water loss
Constipation, anorexia, nausea~30–50%Calcium slows GI smooth-muscle contraction and depresses the CTZ appetite centres
Cognitive slowing, depression, poor concentration~20–40%Hypercalcemia depresses CNS synaptic transmission ("moans")
Nephrolithiasis / nephrocalcinosis~15–20% of PHPTChronic hypercalciuria supersaturates the urine with calcium salts
Bone pain, osteoporosis, fragility fracture~15–20%PTH-driven cortical bone resorption (classically the distal radius)
Peptic ulcer / pancreatitis / abdominal pain<10%Calcium stimulates gastrin & activates pancreatic trypsinogen
Band keratopathy, pruritus<5%Calcium-phosphate precipitation in cornea/skin (chronic, high Ca×PO₄)
Confusion, stupor, coma, arrhythmia<5% (severe only)Seen with Ca ≥14 — a crisis, not a clinic problem (see ICU)
Calcium-containing renal calculi — the "stones" of chronic hypercalcemia/PHPT.

Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The PTH-anchored algorithm

Step 1 — confirm it's real. Repeat the calcium and always pair it with albumin; correct it, or measure ionized calcium if albumin/pH are abnormal. Step 2 — one lab decides the branch: intact PTH.

Corrected Ca / ionized CaConfirm true hypercalcemia. Use ionized Ca when albumin is low, myeloma is suspected, or acid–base is deranged.First
Intact PTHThe pivot. High / inappropriately-normal → PTH-mediated. Low/suppressed → PTH-independent (hunt for a cause).First
Phosphate, Mg, creatinine/eGFRPO₄ low in PHPT & PTHrP (phosphaturia); high in vitamin-D excess/milk-alkali. eGFR sets surgical criteria.First
25-OH & 1,25-OH vitamin DIf PTH is LOW: ↑1,25 = granuloma/lymphoma; ↑25-OH = vitamin D intake. Also check 25-OH before parathyroidectomy.If PTH low
PTHrPIf PTH low and malignancy suspected — elevated confirms humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.If PTH low
24-h urine calcium + creatinine (CCCR)If PTH high — a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 flags FHH (don't operate); >400 mg/day is a surgical criterion.If PTH high
SPEP/UPEP + free light chains, TSH, vit AIf PTH low without an obvious cause — screen myeloma, thyrotoxicosis, hypervitaminosis A.If PTH low
DXA (3 sites incl. distal ⅓ radius) & renal imagingIn PHPT — DXA and renal US/CT define surgical criteria (T-score ≤ −2.5, silent stones/nephrocalcinosis).PHPT staging
Neck US / sestamibi (99mTc)Only after deciding to operate — to localize the adenoma for the surgeon, not to make the diagnosis.Pre-op

How to read the key labs

LabDirectionWhy it moves & what fools you
Intact PTH↑/normal in PHPT; ↓ in malignancyA "normal" PTH with high calcium is inappropriate — a healthy gland should be fully suppressed. Lithium can keep it up.
Corrected calcium↑Low albumin hides true hypercalcemia; every 1 g/dL fall in albumin lowers total Ca ~0.8 mg/dL without changing ionized Ca. Acidosis raises ionized Ca.
Phosphate↓ (PHPT, PTHrP) / ↑ (vit D, milk-alkali)PTH & PTHrP are phosphaturic; vitamin-D and intake states retain phosphate.
1,25-OH vitamin D↑ in granuloma/lymphomaMacrophage 1α-hydroxylase is unregulated by PTH — the tell for sarcoid/TB/lymphoma.
ECG (QTc)Short QT / short STCalcium shortens phase-2 of the action potential; severe cases → bradyarrhythmia, Osborn waves, digoxin sensitivity.
99mTc-sestamibi SPECT-CT localizing a parathyroid adenoma — a pre-operative roadmap, not a diagnostic test.

Corrected calcium & severity

Albumin-corrected total calcium (Payne formula). If albumin or pH is abnormal, confirm with a measured ionized calcium.

—
Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin).

Formula & bands: Payne RB, BMJ 1973; severity cut-offs per Endocrine Society / UpToDate. Cross-check with MDCalc Calcium Correction.

Distinguishing the common look-alikes

When PTH is high, the job is to separate PHPT (operable) from FHH (never operate) and drug effects. When PTH is low, it's about finding the malignant or vitamin-D source. This grid is the quick mental model:

EntityPTHUrine Ca / CCCRPhosphateThe tell & what to do
Primary hyperparathyroidismHigh / high-normalNormal–high; CCCR >0.02Low / low-normalAutonomous adenoma → surgery if criteria met
FHHHigh-normal / mildly highLow; CCCR <0.01NormalLifelong benign CaSR mutation, family history → do NOT operate; genetics
Lithium / thiazideHigh-normal / highLow (thiazide)NormalStop the drug, re-measure calcium & PTH off it
Humoral malignancy (PTHrP)LowHighLowPTHrP ↑; look for squamous/renal/breast tumor; anti-resorptive
Granuloma / lymphomaLowHighNormal / high1,25-OH vit D ↑ → glucocorticoids + treat the cause
Vitamin D toxicity / milk-alkaliLowHighNormal / highStop supplements; milk-alkali = Ca + alkalosis + AKI triad
The trap: a mildly high PTH with a mildly high calcium is not automatically PHPT. Before booking surgery, exclude FHH with the CCCR and a family history, and rule out lithium/thiazide — an unnecessary parathyroidectomy in FHH is a classic, avoidable error.

Calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR)

The PHPT-vs-FHH discriminator when PTH is high. CCCR = (24-h urine Ca × serum Cr) ÷ (serum Ca × 24-h urine Cr) — use consistent units (all mg/dL & mg/dL, or use the same for urine).

—
Enter all four values.

Threshold: CCCR <0.01 supports FHH (confirm with family history / CASR genetics); >0.02 favors PHPT. ~20% of FHH fall in the 0.01–0.02 gray zone (StatPearls, FHH).

Treat

Chronic management — PHPT

💊

Surgery vs medical — first-line → escalation

1
Parathyroidectomy — the only cure
Definitive for symptomatic PHPT and for asymptomatic patients meeting any criterion below.
▾
Removing the autonomous gland restores the CaSR feedback loop — calcium, PTH, BMD and stone risk all normalize. Minimally-invasive parathyroidectomy has a >95% cure rate in experienced hands.

2022 International Workshop surgical criteria (any one):

  • Serum calcium >1.0 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal
  • BMD T-score ≤ −2.5 at any site, or a vertebral fracture on imaging (VFA/X-ray)
  • eGFR/creatinine clearance <60 mL/min
  • 24-h urine calcium >400 mg/day with increased stone risk, or nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis on imaging
  • Age <50 years
Always check & replete 25-OH vitamin D (target >30 ng/mL) before parathyroidectomy — deficiency worsens post-op "hungry bone" hypocalcemia.
2
Medical management — not a surgical candidate / declines
Target the dominant problem: calcium vs bone.
▾

Monitoring alone is appropriate for mild asymptomatic PHPT that doesn't meet criteria. When treating medically, pick the drug by what you're trying to fix:

DrugStartTitration → Target/MaxWhy it worksIf intolerant / notes
Cinacalcet30 mg PO BID↑ q2–4 wk (30→60→90 mg BID); max 90 mg BID (360 mg/day)Calcimimetic — allosteric CaSR agonist lowers PTH & calciumLowers Ca but not BMD; nausea common. Use for calcium control when surgery isn't done.
Alendronate70 mg PO weeklyContinue weekly; reassess DXA q1–2 yrBisphosphonate — inhibits osteoclast resorption, improves spine/hip BMDFor the bone problem; minimal effect on serum Ca. Alt: risedronate 35 mg weekly, IV zoledronic 5 mg yearly.
Cholecalciferol800–1000 IU/day (or repletion dosing if deficient)Target 25-OH D >30 ng/mL; recheck Ca in 4–6 wkCorrects concurrent deficiency, which paradoxically drives PTH higherSafe in PHPT if hypercalcemia is mild; monitor calcium after starting.

General measures: keep calcium intake moderate (~800–1000 mg/day — neither high nor restricted), stay well hydrated, stay physically active (immobilization worsens it), and stop thiazides & lithium where possible and re-measure.

3
Refractory / specialist — parathyroid carcinoma & tertiary HPT
Endocrine surgery + calcimimetics.
▾

Parathyroid carcinoma (rare, very high Ca & PTH) → en-bloc surgical resection; cinacalcet is the mainstay for unresectable/persistent disease (titrate aggressively, often to 90 mg TID–QID under specialist care). Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (autonomous glands after long-standing CKD) → cinacalcet (or etelcalcetide in dialysis) and/or subtotal parathyroidectomy. Refer to endocrinology/endocrine surgery.

📈

What to recheck, and when

SettingWhatHow often
Monitored (non-operative) PHPTSerum calcium & creatinine/eGFRAnnually
Monitored PHPTDXA (3 sites incl. forearm)Every 1–2 years
Monitored PHPTRenal imaging / 24-h urine CaIf stone symptoms or rising calcium
On cinacalcetCalcium (watch for hypocalcemia), PTH1–2 wk after each titration, then q3–6 mo

Prevent

USPSTF A/B & bone health

🛡️

Relevant screening for this population

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BScreen for osteoporosis with bone measurement (DXA) to prevent fractureWomen ≥65; postmenopausal <65 with fracture risk equivalent (USPSTF 2018)
BOsteoporosis screening — men: individualize; formal screening in those with risk factorsRelevant since PHPT is a secondary cause of low BMD
The USPSTF gives vitamin D screening in asymptomatic adults an "I" (insufficient evidence) — so a hypercalcemia work-up is triggered by an incidental calcium or symptoms, not by population screening. There is no USPSTF calcium-screening recommendation.

Bone-protective counselling for PHPT: weight-bearing exercise, fall precautions, adequate but not excessive calcium (~1000 mg/day), maintain vitamin D sufficiency, avoid smoking and excess alcohol.

Escalate

When to send to the ED

🚑

Red flags → same-day admission

Don't manage in clinic — send in — if any of:
  • Corrected/ionized calcium ≥14 mg/dL (hypercalcemic crisis) regardless of symptoms
  • Calcium ≥12 with symptoms — confusion, marked lethargy, intractable vomiting, severe dehydration
  • Acute kidney injury, an arrhythmia, or a shortened QT on ECG
  • Rapidly rising calcium or a newly suspected malignancy driving it
A patient can look deceptively well at 13.5 if it rose slowly — anchor on the number and trajectory, not just how they appear.
🛏️ Wards — acute lowering of calcium
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & severity

BandCorrected CaDisposition
Mild10.5–11.9 mg/dLUsually outpatient; admit only if symptomatic or AKI
Moderate12.0–13.9 mg/dLAdmit if symptomatic, dehydrated, or rising; floor management
Severe / crisis≥14 mg/dLAlways admit; consider ICU (see ICU tab)

Admit any patient who is symptomatic (delirium, vomiting, profound weakness), has AKI, ECG changes, cannot maintain oral intake, or whose calcium is rising quickly. The core inpatient job is volume, then anti-resorptive, while you diagnose the cause.

Treat

Acute management ladder

💊

Rehydrate → osteoclast brake → definitive anti-resorptive

The acute sequence: fast agents (saline, calcitonin) bridge to the slow, durable anti-resorptive (bisphosphonate/denosumab).
1
Volume expansion — isotonic saline
The universal first move; corrects the dehydration that perpetuates hypercalcemia.
▾
Hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic DI → dehydration → the kidney can't excrete calcium. Refilling the tank restores GFR, and the high filtered sodium load drags calcium into the urine (saline calciuresis).
AgentStartTitration → TargetWhy it worksCautions
0.9% saline200–300 mL/h (1–2 L bolus first if hypotensive)Titrate to urine output 100–150 mL/h; typically 3–4 L in first 24 hRestores GFR + drives calciuresisReassess for volume overload in CHF/CKD/elderly; watch Na, K, Mg
FurosemideOnly if volume-overloaded: 10–20 mg IVTitrate to keep patient euvolemic, not to "force" calciuresisBlocks Na-K-2Cl in TAL → adds calciuresisNot routine — routine loops worsen dehydration; give only after repletion for overload
2
Calcitonin — the fast bridge
Works in hours while the bisphosphonate is still ramping up.
▾
Salmon calcitonin brakes osteoclasts and boosts renal calcium excretion — the only agent that lowers calcium within 4–6 h. But receptors downregulate, so it stops working after ~48 h (tachyphylaxis).
DrugStartTitration → MaxEffectNotes
Salmon calcitonin4 IU/kg SC/IM q12hMay ↑ to 8 IU/kg q6–12h if inadequate↓ Ca ~1–2 mg/dL within 4–6 hTachyphylaxis by 48 h — a bridge only. Skin-test/nausea possible.
3
IV bisphosphonate — the durable anti-resorptive
The definitive drug for hypercalcemia of malignancy; give early, works in a few days.
▾
Bisphosphonates concentrate in bone, are ingested by osteoclasts, and inhibit farnesyl-pyrophosphate synthase → osteoclast apoptosis. Onset 2–4 days, nadir 4–7 days, effect lasts 2–4 weeks — so give it with the saline/calcitonin, not after they fail.
DrugDoseRenal adjustmentWhy pickedAdverse / monitor
Zoledronic acid4 mg IV over ≥15 minReduce if CrCl 30–60; avoid if <30 mL/min (nephrotoxic)Most potent; superior normalization vs pamidronate (Major 2001)Acute-phase flu-like reaction, hypocalcemia, rare osteonecrosis of jaw; check renal + dental; hydrate first
Pamidronate60–90 mg IV over 2–4 hPrefer over zoledronic if borderline renal function; infuse slowlyAlternative; longer infusion, slightly less potentSame class effects; slower infusion
Ibandronate2–6 mg IVSometimes used where renal function limits othersAlternative bisphosphonateLess commonly used in the US
4
Denosumab — bisphosphonate-refractory or renal failure
RANKL antibody; not cleared by the kidney.
▾
Denosumab neutralizes RANKL so osteoclasts are never activated. Because it isn't renally cleared, it's the go-to when the bisphosphonate can't be used (CrCl <30–35) or when calcium rebounds after one.
DrugDoseWhy pickedAdverse / monitor
Denosumab120 mg SC (HCM regimen: days 1, 8, 15, 29, then every 4 weeks)Effective in bisphosphonate-refractory HCM; safe in renal failure; median time to response ~9 days (Hu 2014)Watch for delayed, sometimes severe hypocalcemia (higher risk in CKD / vitamin D deficiency) — replete vitamin D & monitor Ca
5
Glucocorticoids — vitamin-D-mediated causes
Sarcoid, other granulomas, lymphoma, vitamin D toxicity.
▾
Steroids inhibit macrophage/lymphoma 1α-hydroxylase → less calcitriol → less gut calcium absorption. They do nothing for PHPT or PTHrP-driven disease, so use them only when the cause is calcitriol-driven.
DrugDoseWhy pickedNotes
Prednisone20–40 mg PO daily × 3–5 days, then taper↓ calcitriol production in granuloma/lymphoma; ↓ gut Ca absorptionAlso treats the underlying lymphoma; onset 2–5 days
Hydrocortisone200–300 mg IV daily × 3–5 daysIV equivalent for the acutely illSame indication set
For moderate–severe hypercalcemia, don't do these one-at-a-time-and-wait. Start saline + calcitonin + a bisphosphonate together: saline and calcitonin drop the calcium within hours; the bisphosphonate takes the baton for the durable fix a few days later.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Corrected/ionized calcium — q6–12 h while actively treating, then daily as it falls.
  • Renal function & electrolytes — saline diuresis wastes K and Mg; replete them (low Mg blocks recovery and blunts calcitonin).
  • Volume status & urine output — target 100–150 mL/h; watch for iatrogenic overload.
  • Phosphate — often needs repletion after treatment, especially with bisphosphonates.
  • Symptoms & mental status — should track the calcium down.
If calcium isn't falling by 24–48 h despite adequate saline + calcitonin + a bisphosphonate, reconsider the diagnosis (is this calcitriol-mediated needing steroids? renal failure needing dialysis?) and escalate.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers

Escalate to critical care for:
  • Calcium ≥18 mg/dL, or ≥14 with severe symptoms (coma, seizure, refractory arrhythmia)
  • Cardiac arrhythmia or hemodynamic instability
  • Oliguric AKI or CHF that can't tolerate the saline load → needs hemodialysis
  • Depressed consciousness with airway concern
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: calcium trending down and <12 mg/dL, symptoms resolved, tolerating oral intake, stable renal function, a definitive anti-resorptive on board, offending drugs stopped, and a plan for the underlying cause (endocrine referral for PHPT; oncology for HCM).

Home

Calcium controlled, independent, follow-up arranged (endocrine/onc).

Home health

Needs labs drawn / infusion follow-up but otherwise independent.

SNF

Deconditioned from prolonged illness; needs skilled nursing & monitoring.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rarely — after prolonged critical illness with reconditioning need.

LTAC

Complex ongoing needs (e.g., cancer with prolonged dependency).

Hospice / palliative

Hypercalcemia of malignancy with poor prognosis — align care with goals; recurrent HCM often marks end-stage disease.
🫀 ICU — hypercalcemic crisis
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Hypercalcemic crisis: calcium ≥14 mg/dL with end-organ dysfunction — depressed consciousness/coma, seizure, cardiac arrhythmia or shortened QT, or oliguric AKI. Very high levels (≥18) are life-threatening irrespective of symptoms.
  • Need for continuous cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia, digoxin toxicity risk)
  • Volume-overload states (CHF, ESRD) that cannot tolerate the aggressive saline needed on the floor → early hemodialysis
  • Airway protection for obtundation
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous telemetry — watch QT, for bradyarrhythmia/heart block, and digoxin effect.
  • Ionized calcium q4–6 h — more reliable than total in critical illness/altered albumin.
  • Central access if giving high-volume resuscitation or planning dialysis; strict I/O and hourly urine output.
  • Frequent BMP — track K, Mg, PO₄ (all wasted by saline diuresis) and renal function.
  • Foley for accurate output while targeting 100–150 mL/h.
Correct magnesium and potassium aggressively — saline calciuresis depletes both, and the resulting hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia compounds the arrhythmia risk from hypercalcemia itself.

💉

The crisis cocktail — combined, not sequential

AgentMechanismDoseOnset / effectWhen to pick

CalcitoninOsteoclast brake + renal Ca excretion4 IU/kg SC/IM q12h (→8 IU/kg q6–12h)4–6 h; ↓1–2 mg/dL; tachyphylaxis 48 hEvery crisis as a bridge

Filter

Hemodialysis for calcium

🩺

Low/zero-calcium bath — the definitive rescue

When calcium must come down now and the usual measures can't be used or aren't fast enough, dialyze against a low- or zero-calcium dialysate. It removes calcium directly and rapidly.

Indication
Severe + renal failure/CHF
or refractory to saline/anti-resorptive, or neuro/cardiac crisis
Modality
HD (or CRRT)
low/zero-Ca bath; CRRT if hemodynamically unstable
Speed
Hours
fastest way to lower calcium
Watch
Rebound + Mg/PO₄
recheck Ca after; anti-resorptive still needed for durable control
Dialysis buys immediate control but doesn't treat the source — pair it with a bisphosphonate/denosumab and definitive management of the underlying cause.
Rescue

Refractory & special situations

⚙️

When the standard ladder fails

  • Bisphosphonate-refractory HCM → denosumab 120 mg SC (Hu 2014: ~64% responded by day 10).
  • Parathyroid carcinoma / inoperable severe PHPT → cinacalcet, titrated aggressively under specialist care.
  • Digoxin toxicity + hypercalcemia → hypercalcemia potentiates digoxin ("stone heart"); avoid IV calcium, treat the hypercalcemia, use digoxin-specific antibody fragments if toxic.
  • Immobilization-driven (e.g., young trauma patient) → bisphosphonate + early mobilization.
  • Definitive source control — urgent parathyroidectomy for parathyroid crisis; treat the tumor for HCM.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Move to the floor when:
  • Calcium is <12 mg/dL and falling, off aggressive interventions
  • Mental status back to baseline, no arrhythmia, ECG normalized
  • Hemodynamically stable, adequate urine output, no further dialysis needed
  • A definitive anti-resorptive has been given and is taking effect
Not yet if: calcium is still ≥14, arrhythmia persists, dialysis is ongoing, or mental status hasn't cleared.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

⚠️

How comorbidities change the plan

ComorbidityEffect on hypercalcemia / management
CKD / renal failureZoledronic acid contraindicated at low CrCl (avoid <30 mL/min; nephrotoxic); prefer denosumab — but denosumab causes severe hypocalcemia more often in CKD. Saline load poorly tolerated → earlier dialysis.
Heart failureAggressive saline can precipitate pulmonary edema — pair with a loop diuretic once repleted, watch closely, dialyze earlier.
On digoxinHypercalcemia potentiates digoxin → arrhythmia ("stone heart"). Avoid IV calcium; monitor levels; correct calcium.
MalignancyHCM signals high tumor burden & poor prognosis — treat the calcium but revisit goals of care; recurrence is common.
Vitamin D deficiency (with PHPT)Deficiency drives PTH higher; replete before surgery and before denosumab to prevent post-treatment hypocalcemia.
NephrolithiasisA single surgical criterion for PHPT — its presence changes monitoring into an operative indication.
Drugs to stop / avoid in active hypercalcemia:
  • Thiazide diuretics — reduce urinary calcium excretion (raise calcium).
  • Lithium — shifts the CaSR set-point, raising PTH & calcium.
  • Calcium & vitamin D supplements, calcium-based antacids (milk-alkali), vitamin A.
  • Volume depletion / prolonged immobilization — both worsen it.
  • Routine loop diuretics (old teaching) — only after volume repletion, only for overload.
  • In digoxin toxicity — avoid IV calcium.
Pearls

Pearls & pitfalls

💡

The high-yield takeaways & classic traps

Correct before you react. Always albumin-correct or measure ionized calcium first — hypoalbuminemia hides true hypercalcemia. A total of 9.6 mg/dL at an albumin of 2.0 is really a corrected 11.2 — genuinely hypercalcemic. Conversely, a "high" total with a high albumin can be pseudohypercalcemia.
PTH is the fork in the road. One lab splits the entire differential: high/inappropriately-normal PTH → PTH-mediated (think PHPT); suppressed PTH → PTH-independent (hunt malignancy, granuloma, vitamin D). Draw it before treatment blurs the picture.
Two causes are 90%. Primary hyperparathyroidism dominates the clinic; malignancy dominates the hospital — and hypercalcemia of malignancy is a poor-prognosis marker worth a goals-of-care conversation.
CCCR < 0.01 → think FHH, and do NOT operate. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is a benign CaSR mutation; a parathyroidectomy won't cure it. Check a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio and a family history before sending anyone to surgery.
Volume, volume, volume. The dehydrated hypercalcemic patient needs isotonic saline first — it's the single most important early move, correcting the nephrogenic-DI dehydration that perpetuates the high calcium.
Never give a loop diuretic to a dry patient. The old "saline + furosemide forced diuresis" teaching is out — loops in a volume-depleted patient worsen hypercalcemia. Reserve them for volume overload after full repletion.
Give calcitonin AND the bisphosphonate together, up front. Calcitonin works in hours but fades by 48 h (tachyphylaxis); the bisphosphonate takes 2–4 days to work but lasts weeks. Sequencing them wastes the bridge — run them in parallel.
Renal failure flips the drug choice. Zoledronic acid is nephrotoxic and contraindicated at low CrCl — reach for denosumab (not renally cleared), but anticipate delayed, sometimes severe hypocalcemia, especially in CKD and vitamin D deficiency.
Steroids only help the calcitriol-driven causes. Prednisone works for sarcoid/granuloma, lymphoma, and vitamin D toxicity — and does nothing for PHPT or PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia. Match the drug to the mechanism.
Phosphate points the way. Low phosphate → PTH or PTHrP (both phosphaturic); normal/high phosphate → calcitriol-mediated, milk-alkali, or immobilization.
Watch the heart. Short QT is the classic ECG sign; hypercalcemia potentiates digoxin ("stone heart") — avoid IV calcium in a digoxin-toxic patient and monitor telemetry when calcium is high.
Replete vitamin D before you cut or before denosumab. Deficiency drives PTH higher and worsens post-parathyroidectomy "hungry bone" and denosumab-related hypocalcemia — target 25-OH-D >30 ng/mL first.
Hungry bone syndrome — after parathyroidectomy for severe long-standing PHPT, the suddenly PTH-deprived, avid skeleton can pull calcium, phosphate and magnesium out of the blood for days. Monitor calcium closely post-op and replete aggressively.
